A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, In-context learning and Occam’s razor. All 23 pages of v2 and 21 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on regression, Mastermind, and HMM tasks, including architecture, regularization, task-difficulty, and context-length comparisons.

after.justification: v3 retains original regression and Mastermind experiments and reports additional HMM architecture and learning-objective comparisons in Figure 2b and Appendix F.

M1.justification: The core prequential ICL objective and learner architectures remain unchanged. However, v3 removes the proposed short-context-biased training strategy from v2 Section 3.5 and Appendix E.4.5, eliminating a complementary procedural contribution.

E1.justification: The regression, Mastermind, and HMM data families remain. Appendix F adds a supervised HMM scenario that supplies time indices as inputs and tests prediction of subsequent observations, extending v2’s sequence-based HMM evaluation.

E2.justification: On the retained HMM family, v3 evaluates bottlenecked and unbottlenecked Transformers against Mamba 1 and Mamba 2 in Figure 2b; v2 compared uniform and short-context-biased Transformer training in Figure 3b. Comparator memberships in the retained iid and GPT-4 experiments are unchanged.

E3.justification: The HMM protocol changes substantially: v2 specifies 11,228 training and 1,000 held-out HMMs, a six-layer Transformer, and reverse-KL evaluation. v3 reports 60,000 training and 13,728 held-out latent compositions, shared four-layer architectures, and cross-entropy evaluation. Appendix F introduces time-index queries. These are revised or new settings, not same-setting performance comparisons.

E4.justification: v3 removes the context-length sampling study and its training-convergence analyses from v2 Section 3.5 and Figures E.2–E.3. It adds nonstationary HMM comparisons of architectures and learning objectives, including the train-risk and SGD controls in Appendix F. The task-difficulty and regularization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages and standard errors using five seeds for ICL and fifteen for SGD. The additional HMM comparisons follow this existing practice; no changed repetition counts or new uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported.

E6.justification: v3 adds HMM findings favoring SSMs over Transformers and prequential ICL over train-risk ICL and SGD in the supervised HMM setting. It removes the short-context training advantage and the finding that uniform-context training catches up by 610 million tokens. The retained iid, GPT-4, task-difficulty, and regularization results are unchanged.

T1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.2 replace the iid, per-observation formulation with a dataset likelihood p(D) and ordered data, broadening the formal assumptions. Appendix A also removes the lower bound in Equation (15), revises its equality condition, and drops the large-dataset qualification preceding Equation (17). The central prequential bound and Appendix B derivation remain.

C1.justification: v2 explicitly limits its theoretical framework to iid data and leaves nonstationary generalization for future work. v3 Section 2.4 and the conclusion claim applicability to both iid and nonstationary data, substantially broadening the theory’s stated scope. The central connection between ICL, compression, and Occam’s razor remains.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the iid-only limitation with discussion of data ordering and curricula. It adds explanations of architecture–task interactions and of online ICL succeeding where train-risk controls fail on nonstationary sequences. The short-context mechanism discussion and its eventual-convergence qualification are removed.

D1.justification: The HMM-specific implementation description is revised to reference shared model and training settings, and Appendix F discloses the time-index transformation and relative positional encodings. Oracle-evaluation and short-context implementation passages disappear. Other architecture details, GPT-4 prompting instructions, and the code-access link remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds Lampinen et al. (2024) to distinguish forms of ICL, Shaw et al. (2018) for relative positions, and Zhang et al. (2020) for information transfer and ordering. The main research positioning and Bayesian comparison remain; the extensive bibliography formatting changes do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the appendices: experimental details move from E to C, task difficulty from C to D, and Bayesian discussion from D to G; regularization becomes a separate Appendix E. Section 3.5 disappears, and the introduction and nonstationary-data explanations are revised, although much retained prose is unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 consolidates v2’s GPT-4 panel into Figure 2c and adds an HMM architecture panel to Figure 2b. It removes Figure 3b and Figures E.2–E.3, adds Figure F.1, and relocates existing appendix displays. The main experimental figure is substantially rearranged and resized.

improvement.justification: v3 clarifies ICL’s scope and adds useful nonstationary controls, while removing v2’s practical short-context study. However, Appendix C.4 retains a total of 12,228 HMMs while reporting 60,000 training and 13,728 held-out compositions, leaving the new experiments’ specification inconsistent. The added support, reduced practical evidence, and unresolved reproducibility problem do not establish a reliable net quality improvement or deterioration.
